title: Father of Modern Management
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 2

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–27, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

Father of Modern Management

Paragraph A

A A Peter Drucker was one of the most important management thinkers of the past hundred years. He wrote about 40 books and thousands of articles. Wherever people grapple with tricky management problems, you can find Drucker's fingerprints.

Paragraph B

B B His first two books—The End of Economic Man (1939) and The Future of Industrial Man (1942)—had their admirers, including Winston Churchill, but they annoyed academic critics by ranging so widely over so many different subjects. Still, the second of these books attracted attention with its passionate insistence that companies had a social dimension as well as an economic purpose. His third book, The Concept of the Corporation, became an instant bestseller and has remained in print ever since.

Paragraph C

C C The two most interesting arguments in The Concept of the Corporation actually had little to do with the decentralization fad. They were to dominate his work. The first had to do with “empowering” workers. Drucker believed in treating workers as resources rather than just as costs. He was a harsh critic of the assemblyline system of production that then dominated the manufacturing sector—partly because assembly lines moved at the speed of the slowest and partly because they failed to engage the creativity of individual workers. The second argument had to do with the rise of knowledge workers. Drucker argued that the world is moving from an ‘economy of goods’ to an ‘economy of knowledge’—and from a society dominated by an industrial proletariat to one dominated by brain workers. He insisted that this had profound implications for both managers and politicians. Managers had to stop treating workers like cogs in a huge inhuman machine and start treating them as brain workers. In turn, politicians had to realise that knowledge, and hence education, was the single most important resource for any advanced society. Yet Drucker also thought that this economy had implications for knowledge workers themselves. They had to come to terms with the fact that they were neither ‘bosses’ nor ‘workers’, but something in between: entrepreneurs who had responsibility for developing their most important resource, brainpower, and who also needed to take more control of their own careers, including their pension plans.

Paragraph D

D D This work contained a difficult side, though. One of the most successful products of the National School of Management, ‘management by objectives,’ was invented by Drucker. He claimed that longterm objectives should be set by managers and companies, and the objectives must be translated into more immediate outcomes in his most substantial book The Practice of Management (1954). Specialised managers should work to achieve the longterm goals set by a more elite group of general managers. Before, he had emphasized the importance of softer management, and critics viewed this development as a retreat. Drucker thought that relying too heavily on command and control risked sacrificing creativity, but that allowing too much empowerment ran the risk of creating anarchy, so this approach was natural and consistent. Managers should encourage employees to devise their own methods of meeting goals, but only after the managers themselves devised the longterm goals the employees would progress toward. Drucker helped to expand management beyond its original base in business as he was helping to make it a worldwide industry. He came from business, but he was very much interested in management's broader conceptual implications. He thought that management could apply to all big bureaucracies, not just corporations, calling it ‘the defining organ of all modern institutions’.

Paragraph E

E E Drucker's ideas draw three recurring critiques. His focus on large organisations instead of smaller ones is the first. Big organisations treated The Concept of the Corporation as a fanfare. ‘Small units are not just inefficient, they are incapable of production in today's industrial production landscape,’ Drucker wrote. The ‘big organisation boom’ that consumed thinking about business for the next two decades was launched in part by Drucker's book. His promotion of management by objectives caused businesses to pursue dead ends, according to the second major criticism of Drucker's work. Ideas should come from the middle or the bottom of large organisations instead of coming as an imposition from the top, according to them. A third criticism is that the increasingly rigorous field that Drucker chose has left no place for a maverick like him. He has not made any one type of academic management theory his specialty.

Paragraph F

F F The first two criticisms are at least partly valid. There was no version of The Concept of the Corporation written with equal quality about entrepreneurship or startups. His early and late work about selfdirected units and the value of knowledge workers seems in contrast with his description of management by objectives. The final criticism ignores Drucker's important contribution to the creation of what we understand as professional management, and the argument is not fair or longsighted. It might seem banal today to review his remarks about the value of empowerment and the virtues of knowledge workers. When these ideas emerged from Drucker's mind in the 1940s, they were not banal at all, however, and certainly not in the 1980s when they became standard practice in the West.
